sections.title: Background facts used in the book

blocks.x: We list the results from other courses that we used without proof.
If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ then $\frac{\dd}{\dd x}\int_a^xf=f(x)$, and $\int_a^bf'=f(b)-f(a)$ for $f\in C^1$.
If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable inside, then $f(b)-f(a)=f'(c)(b-a)$ for some $c\in(a,b)$.
A continuous function on a closed bounded set of $\R^n$ is bounded, attains its maximum and minimum, and is uniformly continuous.

$\det(AB)=\det A\det B$; $\det A\neq0$ iff $A$ is invertible; $\abs{\det A}$ is the volume scaling factor; $\det$ is multilinear and alternating in the columns; $\frac{\dd}{\dd t}\det A=\det A\,\tr(A^{-1}\dot A)$.
A real symmetric matrix has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors with real eigenvalues. It is positive definite iff all eigenvalues are positive.

If $T:X\to X$ is a contraction ($d(Tx,Ty)\le q\,d(x,y)$, $q<1$) on a complete metric space, then $T$ has a unique fixed point, found as the limit of $x,Tx,T^2x,\dots$ (used in the inverse function theorem, Chapter 2).
If $f$ and $\partial_tf$ are continuous on $[a,b]\times[c,d]$, then $\frac{\dd}{\dd t}\int_a^bf(x,t)\dd x=\int_a^b\partial_tf\,\dd x$ (Theorem 4.14).
For $f$ continuous on a rectangle, iterated integrals in either order give the double integral (Theorem 4.3).
